articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This action reflects ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy concerning Venezuela.

The specifics of the amended General License and the new FAQ were not immediately detailed in the announcement, but such updates typically clarify permissible activities or provide guidance on existing restrictions within the Venezuela sanctions program.

These changes are part of the dynamic U.S. approach to Venezuela, which has seen both designations and removals in recent months, often tied to diplomatic efforts and negotiations regarding the country's political landscape.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian and Cuban Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on these actions.

The Iran-related designations targeted two offshore banks affiliated with Bank Mellat and Bank Shahr, an Iraqi bank, and a network of exchange houses, commercial companies, and revenue transfer intermediaries involved in Iranian oil sales. These actions are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aiming to cut off Iran's access to foreign currency and international banking networks.

Additionally, Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) was designated due to its ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank, which has been under sanctions since 2020. The U.S. State Department emphasized that Cuba has been operating as an outpost for malign actors, including Iran.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Africanews / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodríguez from Sanctions List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Rodríguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its sanctions list on October 14, 2026. This delisting ends broad prohibitions on U.S. dealings with Rodríguez and lifts any asset freezes under U.S. jurisdiction.

Rodríguez, who has led the Venezuelan parliament since 2021, was originally designated in September 2018 during the first Trump administration. His removal from the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist is seen as a significant step in warming relations between Washington and Caracas.

This move follows a broader diplomatic shift and comes amid U.S.-backed talks in Caracas that are pivoting more directly to elections. Earlier this year, sanctions were also lifted on Delcy Rodríguez, Jorge's sister and Venezuela's interim president, as well as on Venezuela's central bank and state-owned airline Conviasa.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Al Jazeera / AFP

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit activities that threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy.
Such designations aim to disrupt the financial networks of those engaged in drug trafficking and terrorism, thereby limiting their ability to operate and fund their illicit operations globally.

The U.S. Treasury Department regularly employs these targeted sanctions to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist groups, reinforcing international efforts to counter these threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates International Criminal Court Officials, Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) on October 9, 2026. This action was accompanied by the issuance of new General Licenses.
These designations typically target individuals or entities associated with the ICC, reflecting U.S. policy concerns regarding the court's jurisdiction or actions.
The accompanying General Licenses aim to mitigate any unintended consequences of the designations, allowing for certain transactions or activities to continue under specific conditions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This action provides specific authorizations for certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.
General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to clarify the scope of sanctions, facilitate humanitarian aid, or allow for wind-down periods for certain business operations.
This new General License is part of the ongoing adjustments to the extensive U.S. sanctions regime targeting Russia in response to its actions in Ukraine.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Iran-Related Designations and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued an Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License.

The Iran-related designations are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' to disrupt the Iranian regime's financial networks and illicit activities. These actions often target entities involved in Iran's shadow fleet network and other sectors supporting the regime.
The amended Russia-related General License indicates a refinement of existing sanctions, potentially adjusting the scope of permissible activities or providing further clarity for compliance.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Alert to Foreign Financial Institutions on Iran Sanctions Risk
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations removals and updates, and published an Iran-related OFAC Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question on October 5, 2026.

The OFAC Alert specifically warns foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions that they 'could be targeted at any time without advance notification.' This alert is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' launched to sever financial resources supporting the Iranian regime.

Furthermore, OFAC amended Iran-related FAQ 156, removing previous language that suggested FFIs would generally receive advance contact before being found to have knowingly engaged in sanctionable activity. This change signals a more aggressive enforcement posture by OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026. These actions are aimed at disrupting the financial support networks of terrorist organizations globally.
Such designations typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting transactions with the designated individuals and entities, thereby isolating them from the international financial system.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating terrorism and protecting national security interests through financial sanctions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts Largest-Ever Package of Russia Sanctions, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, marking its largest single round of designations ever. This package adds a record 1,646 natural persons and legal entities to the EU's sanctions lists, bringing the total number of designations under this regime to nearly 4,600.

The new designations primarily target individuals and entities viewed as core players of Russia's military industry, including 826 Russian companies and 743 executives linked to the military-industrial complex. The measures also include individuals involved in elections for the Russian State Duma in occupied Ukrainian territories.

These expanded listings entail the freezing of assets and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available to them, with individuals also subject to a travel ban to the EU. The EU emphasized its growing reliance on targeted designations to increase pressure on Russia and address sanctions circumvention.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Morgan Lewis / Steptoe

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Three Individuals and Four Entities Over DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs, Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on October 12, 2026. These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs.

The new listings also address violations and evasion of United Nations sanctions, specifically targeting activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia. This includes the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

The EU reiterated its firm commitment to the full implementation of UN sanctions against the DPRK and called on Pyongyang to comply with its obligations to abandon its weapons programs in a complete, verifiable, and irreversible manner.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Consilium.europa.eu

articles.headline: President Trump Waives Key Sanctions from Lindsey O. Graham Act Targeting Russia and Iran
body: President Donald Trump issued an executive order on October 16, 2026, waiving major sanctions and tariffs established under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The Act, signed into law on September 18, 2026, aimed to impose additional pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine and extended the Iran Sanctions Act.

The waiver suspends measures including an additional 500% tariff on Russian goods and 100% tariffs on imports from countries meeting specified criteria for Russian energy purchases or sanctions evasion. It also covered new restrictions concerning Russian financial institutions, investment, energy transactions, and sovereign debt.

The decision, made days before the October 18 deadline for implementing the additional tariffs, drew outrage from members of Congress who had overwhelmingly passed the legislation. The White House stated the waiver was in the national interest, and it remains effective until the President or Secretary of State determines further action is appropriate.
articles.source: The Guardian / The Moscow Times / Steptoe

This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring financial institutions maintain robust compliance programs to prevent sanctions breaches.
The settlement underscores the importance for large financial institutions to diligently screen transactions and adhere to all applicable sanctions programs to avoid significant penalties.

This enforcement action demonstrates OFAC's commitment to holding companies accountable for their compliance with sanctions programs, regardless of their size or industry.
Companies involved in international logistics and shipping are particularly vulnerable to sanctions risks and must implement effective compliance measures to prevent illicit transactions.

The penalty serves as a reminder that personal accountability for sanctions compliance is a critical aspect of U.S. enforcement efforts.

The case serves as a critical reminder for multinational companies to meticulously review their supply chains, business partners, and operational jurisdictions to ensure full compliance with all applicable U.S. sanctions laws.

Brokerage firms must implement robust compliance controls to identify and block transactions involving sanctioned individuals, entities, or jurisdictions.

Individuals engaged in international transactions or business dealings must be acutely aware of and comply with all U.S. sanctions programs to avoid severe financial and legal repercussions.

articles.headline: U.S. Residential Electricity Rates Rise 5% Year-Over-Year in October 2026
body: The average U.S. residential electricity rate reached 18.34¢/kWh as of October 2026, marking a 5.0% increase year-over-year. This rise contributes to an overall 23% increase in U.S. electricity rates since 2022, adding approximately $440 annually to the average household electric bill.

Electricity rates vary significantly across states, ranging from 13.11 cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in Nevada to 52.72 cents per kWh in Hawaii. Hawaii experienced the largest residential rate increase at +28.7% year-over-year, followed by Idaho (+19.1%) and Washington (+15.0%).

The South Central region remains the cheapest for electricity at 14.47¢/kWh, while the Northeast is the most expensive at 25.49¢/kWh. These regional differences are influenced by fuel sources, infrastructure age, and regulatory structures.

articles.headline: U.S.-Mexico Tariff Deal Stalls Amid Disagreements on Auto and Metal Levies
body: Progress toward a U.S.-Mexico tariff deal has stalled due to opposition from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, according to reports on October 16, 2026. The deal aimed to reduce U.S. levies on steel, aluminum, and automobiles in return for concessions from Mexico.

Secretary Lutnick has reportedly opposed significant reductions in the 25% tariff on Mexican automobiles and the 50% levies on steel and aluminum. He also objected to reductions in tariffs on finished products made of steel and aluminum.
This disagreement has slowed negotiations, despite efforts to work out a trade deal with Mexico, a major producer of vehicles for the U.S. market.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for widespread violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This represents the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with a transaction monitoring system that failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This resulted in the bank filing a large number of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many of which showed indicia of money laundering.

This action was taken in coordination with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which assessed a $1.2 billion fine against Bank of America, crediting the OCC's $750 million penalty. The OCC emphasized that banks are expected to maintain effective BSA/AML compliance programs, and those that do not will face swift and significant action.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) / U.S. Department of the Treasury

articles.headline: OCC Releases Report on Large Banks' 'Debanking' Activities and Industry-Specific Policies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report on October 14, 2026, detailing its findings on the 'debanking' practices of the nine largest national banks it supervises. The report, titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' concludes that these banks maintained policies or practices that may have influenced the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities between 2020 and September 2025.

The OCC found that banks maintained public and nonpublic policies restricting certain industry sectors' access to financial services. These sectors include oil and gas exploration, coal mining or coal-powered plants, firearms or ammunition manufacturing or distribution, and digital asset activities.

This report follows an executive order issued by President Trump last year, directing federal banking regulators to review institutions for politicized or unlawful debanking. The OCC did not announce any enforcement actions or penalties in conjunction with this report, but the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) announced it would investigate compliance with federal consumer financial laws.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
